name: Feature Flags
intent: Ship code to production switched off, then turn it on for chosen users at runtime, gradually, and turn it off again in seconds without a deploy.
scenario: A new checkout page is finished. Instead of releasing it to every shopper at once, the team deploys it dark behind a flag called new-checkout, shows it to 10% of users, then 50%, kills it when errors spike, and finally deletes the flag once it is at 100%.
problem: When deploying and releasing are the same event, every deploy is a gamble: the new page reaches everyone immediately, and the only way back is another deploy or a rollback that takes minutes to hours and may also revert unrelated fixes. Long-lived branches that wait for the feature to be 'ready' make merges painful, and nobody can try the change on a small group first.

howItWorks.title: Deploy the code dark
howItWorks.text: The new checkout page ships to production inside an if: if the flag is on show the new page, otherwise the old one. The flag defaults to off, so deploying changes nothing for users. Deploy (code reaches servers) and release (users see it) become two separate decisions.

howItWorks.title: Evaluate the flag at runtime
howItWorks.text: On each request the app asks an SDK 'is new-checkout on for this user?'. The SDK usually holds the flag rules in memory, fetched at start-up and kept fresh by streaming or polling every few seconds, so evaluation is a local function call that takes microseconds, not a network hop per request.

howItWorks.title: Roll out by percentage with a stable hash
howItWorks.text: To expose 10% of users, hash the flag key plus the user id into a number from 0 to 9999 and turn the flag on when the number is below 1000. The same user always gets the same bucket, so the choice is sticky, and a good hash spreads users evenly. Raising 10% to 50% only adds users: nobody who already had the feature loses it.

howItWorks.title: Add targeting rules
howItWorks.text: Rules are checked before the percentage, in order: staff always on, a country blocked for legal reasons always off, a beta list on. The first matching rule wins, and users matching no rule fall through to the percentage. This lets you test with employees first and exclude groups that are not ready.

howItWorks.title: Keep a kill switch and a safe default
howItWorks.text: A kill switch turns the feature off for everyone within seconds, with no deploy. If the flag service cannot be reached, the SDK keeps using its last known rules, and if it never had any, it uses the default compiled into the code, which should be the safe (usually old) behaviour.

howItWorks.title: Delete the flag when the rollout is done
howItWorks.text: Once the flag has been at 100% long enough to trust it, remove the if, the old page and the flag itself. Flags left behind are debt: every one doubles the paths through the code and nobody remembers which value is the real one. Give each release flag an owner and an expiry date when it is created.

pros: Deploying and releasing are decoupled, so code can merge to main early and often
Gradual exposure limits the damage of a bad change to a small share of users
A kill switch is much faster than a rollback: seconds instead of a pipeline run
Targeting lets staff, beta users or one region try a feature first
Sticky bucketing gives each user a consistent experience across requests and servers
cons: Every flag adds a branch, so tests and reasoning must cover both paths
Flags that are never removed pile up as debt and become hidden configuration
Needs a flag service or config system, with its own availability and access control
Percentage rollouts hash by user, so anonymous visitors without a stable id cannot be bucketed consistently
A flag change is a production change that can break things, so it needs audit logs and permissions like a deploy
whenToUse: Risky or user-visible changes that you want to release gradually and measure
Long-running work that must merge to main before it is finished (trunk-based development)
Features that need an instant off switch, such as a new payment path or an expensive recommendation call
Experiments and per-customer or per-region entitlements
whenNotToUse: Tiny changes with no user-visible risk, where the flag costs more than the change
Changes that cannot sit behind an if, such as an incompatible database schema or a library upgrade; use expand and contract migrations or canary deployments instead
As a permanent substitute for configuration or a permission system: use a proper setting or entitlement for that
When nobody will own removal: an unowned flag is future debt
pitfalls: Randomising per request (Math.random) instead of hashing the user id: the same shopper sees the new page, then the old one, then the new one on refresh
Reusing one salt for every flag, so the same 10% of users are the guinea pigs for every experiment; include the flag key in the hash
Changing the salt or the key mid-rollout, which reshuffles everyone and silently flips users who already saw the feature
Making the flag service a hard dependency on the request path, so its outage becomes your outage; cache rules and define a safe default
Choosing a default that is unsafe: a flag guarding a half-built feature must default to off when the lookup fails
Never deleting release flags, and testing only the 'on' path; the 'off' path is the one you fall back to at 3 a.m.
Evaluating a flag at different points in one request, so half the page is new and half is old

roles.label: Shopper
roles.description: The user whose request is evaluated against the flag.

roles.label: Checkout app
roles.description: Serves the checkout page and holds the flag SDK, which evaluates rules locally from its in-memory copy.

roles.label: Flag service
roles.description: Stores flag definitions (percentage, rules, kill switch) and pushes or serves updates to SDKs.

roles.label: Engineer
roles.description: Deploys code and changes flag settings, two separate actions.

quiz.question: A team rolls out a new product page to 10 percent of users. The flag code calls Math.random() on each request. Users report that the page flips between old and new design when they refresh. What is the best fix?
options: Cache the random result in the browser for one hour, so that a refresh shows the same design.
Hash the flag key and user id into a bucket, and show the page if the bucket is in range.
Lower the rollout to 5 percent, so that fewer of the users see the design flipping back and forth.
Choose the bucket from the server name, so that each server is either fully on or fully off.
quiz.explanation: A stable hash of the user id gives the same answer on every request and every server. A cached random value is lost when the browser clears it, and server-based buckets would flip users as the load balancer moves them.

quiz.question: A checkout service asks a flag service over HTTP on every request. One afternoon the flag service gets slow, and checkout latency doubles even though no flag changed. What is the best change?
options: Raise the checkout timeout to match the flag service's slow responses, so that lookups stop failing.
Retry each failed flag lookup three times with backoff before falling back to the default value.
Add a second flag service in another region and call both of them for every flag lookup.
Evaluate rules in memory in an SDK kept fresh by streaming or polling, with a safe default.
quiz.explanation: Evaluating flags locally from cached rules removes the network hop from the request path, so a flag outage cannot become a checkout outage. Retries and longer timeouts make the dependency worse, and a second service is still on the request path.

quiz.question: Three experiments each run at 10 percent. All three bucket users with a hash of the user id only. A dashboard shows the same 10 percent of users have lower conversion in every experiment. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: The experiments really are all harmful to conversion, so roll each of them back one by one.
The hash is too slow and delays page rendering for those users, so switch to a faster one.
The same users land in every group, so effects stack on one cohort; add the flag key to the hash.
Ten percent is too small a sample for useful statistics, so raise every rollout to 50 percent.
quiz.explanation: Without the flag key as part of the hash, each flag selects the same users, so effects stack on one group and cannot be told apart. Salting by flag key gives each experiment an independent sample.
